about.heading: Mechanical engineering student who works where the drawing meets the machine.
about._paragraphsNote: The first paragraph is the personal one — rewrite it so it sounds like you, not like me. Keep it to two or three sentences; the photo does the rest of the work.
paragraphs: That's me in the photograph, installing my own training wheels. The method has improved since; the instinct has not. I want to know how a thing works, and I would rather find out with my hands than read about it.

It is most of why I chose mechanical engineering, and why the work I am proudest of is the work where I had to make the part and not only draw it. I am a mechanical engineering student at UMass Amherst graduating in May 2027, and most of what I do sits on both sides of a design: modeling and analyzing, building, running the test, and finding out whether the numbers held.

At NexTek I designed a leak test fixture for our largest customer's RF surge protectors: sized four pneumatic cylinders to apply 42.5 psi, built it on 80/20 with an A36 steel cross bar, and took the bench from 4 units per cycle to 16. Every position vents to its own numbered tube in a water bath, so a leak names the unit that failed. More than 21,000 units have gone through it. At Amazon's Reliability and Maintenance Engineering organization, I implemented and validated a PLC-controlled tote-turner using pneumatic actuators and photoelectric sensors, and built a full-stack tracking application on AWS so conveyor sorter amnesty could finally be root-caused with data instead of guesses.

As the Fuel System Lead on the UMass Supermileage Vehicle Team, I replaced a 3.2 lb pressurised air assembly that had cracked and leaked, with a 2 L PET charge bottle and a single machined aluminium adapter — 89% lighter, with far fewer interfaces to fail. The car ran 414 mpg at the Shell Eco-marathon. I also rebuilt a totaled Mazda3 in an apartment parking garage, which taught me more about tolerance and patience than any lab.

projects.title: Fuel Delivery System — Supermileage Vehicle
projects.blurb: A pressure-fed fuel system: 50 psi from a 2 L PET charge bottle pressurises the fuel reservoir, which supplies port injection. The assembly it replaced had cracked, leaked at multiple interfaces, and weighed 3.2 lb against the bottle's 42 g. Validated in Ansys, machined with the University's CNC, then pressure-tested. The car ran 414 mpg at Indianapolis —— beating the previous year's 0 mpg.

problem: A supermileage vehicle only wins on efficiency, so every gram of unnecessary structure and every milliliter of poorly delivered fuel shows up in the final mileage number.

The system I inherited worked against both. It carried too many points of failure: it had cracked, it leaked at multiple interfaces, and at roughly 3.2 lb it was heavy for what it actually had to do — hold pressurized air and hand it to the fuel reservoir.
projects.roleDetail: Fuel System Lead. I own the design and optimisation of the fuel delivery system, coordinate with the wider Engine Sub-team on packaging and integration, and did the CAD, analysis, machining, and testing on the charge bottle and adapter myself.
approach: Traced the previous design's failures back to interface count and material choice — every additional joint was a leak path, and carrying them safely was what made the assembly heavy.

Reduced the pressure side to two parts: a 2 L PET bottle as the air charge vessel, and a single custom aluminium adapter carrying the NPT hose connection into the circuit that pressurises the fuel reservoir.

Chose the bottle deliberately, not as a shortcut: at 42 g it is a mass-produced pressure vessel already qualified for carbonation pressure, which removed both the weight and most of the interfaces in one move.
Modeled the adapter in CAD, validated it in Ansys under pressure and stress, and 3D printed for fitment before cutting any metal.
Programmed the toolpaths and CNC-machined the adapter from stock aluminium, then deburred and verified fitment.
Pressure-tested the assembly by charging the bottle to 50 psi and tracking the leak over two days.
Applied CAD and FEA across the wider fuel delivery system to improve combustion efficiency and structural integrity while trimming mass.
results: Cut pressure vessel mass by 89.8% — from a 3.2 lb (1,450 g) assembly to a 42 g PET charge bottle and a 106 g adapter.
Held 40 of 50 psi after 48 hours, against a previous design that leaked at multiple interfaces.
Removed the crack and multi-interface leak paths by cutting part count rather than adding sealing.
Cost less in material and machining time than the assembly it replaced, and was faster to build.
Vehicle achieved 414 mpg in competition at the Shell Eco-marathon.

projects.title: 16-Up Leak Test Fixture for RF Surge Protectors
projects.blurb: Our old bench tested four units per 10-second cycle, and our largest customer orders tens of thousands at a time — so the test bench set the pace, not the line. I sized four pneumatic cylinders to clamp sixteen units at once at 42.5 psi, built the frame from 80/20 extrusion and an A36 steel cross bar, and ran every station to its own numbered tube in a water bath. One bubble now names the unit that failed.
projects.role: Design, pneumatic sizing, build, and validation owner

specs.value: Four pneumatic cylinders on a two-button control

specs.label: Platens
specs.value: Four lower platens, four units each, with a driven upper platen per cylinder

specs.label: Brackets and fasteners

problem: Our largest customer, a Fortune 500 buyer, orders IP-rated RF surge protectors tens of thousands of units at a time and supplies the spec sheet those units are tested against. Every one has to hold pressure above their spec threshold before it ships.
The method we had could pressure-test four units per 10-second cycle. At that order volume, the test bench — not the line — decided how fast product left the building.

So the fixture had to do three things: apply more pressure than the spec demands with defensible margin, apply it to far more units per cycle, and still tell us which unit failed rather than only that one had. All of it while carrying roughly 680 lbf of reaction load without deflecting enough to break a seal.
projects.roleDetail: I owned the fixture end to end — the pneumatic sizing, the CAD, the FEA, the build, and the validation — alongside roughly four concurrent projects.
approach: Took the requirement straight off the customer's spec sheet, then researched pneumatic cylinders against it — working through bore size, rod diameter, and maximum output to land on a cylinder that applies 42.5 psi at the unit. That is a factor of safety of 1.3 over the spec threshold, which their sheet accepts.
Split the sixteen stations across four lower platens holding four units each, and put a driven upper platen on every cylinder so all sixteen seal in a single stroke.
Put actuation behind two green buttons, so all four cylinders fire together and the operator's hands stay clear of the platens as they close.

Ran every station to its own numbered tube ending below the surface of a water reservoir. A leaking unit bubbles its own tube, so one bubble names the unit rather than the batch — nobody re-tests the other fifteen to find it.
Built the structure from 80/20 aluminium extrusion and an A36 mild steel U-channel cross bar, which carries the clamping load across all sixteen stations without bowing in the middle.
Used aluminium brackets for the supports and 1/4-20 Phillips screws and nuts throughout, so the fixture can be adjusted or serviced with one driver and one wrench.
Ran FEA on the assembly to confirm it carries roughly 680 lbf without deflecting enough to break a seal.
Assembled and validated the fixture on the bench with data acquisition, then put production volume through it.
Fed build issues back through ECOs and change control to keep it in spec as it was used.
results: Throughput went from 4 units per 10-second cycle to 16 — a 300% increase at the same cycle time.
Applied 42.5 psi at the unit, a factor of safety of 1.3 over the customer's spec threshold.
Each numbered tube pins a failure to one unit, so we stopped re-testing whole batches to find it.
FEA confirmed the frame carries roughly 680 lbf without losing seal.
More than 21,000 units have gone through it in production.

projects.title: Rebuild of a Salvage 2008 Mazda3 S
projects.blurb: A salvage car brought back to running order: full mechanical and structural assessment, front-end reconstruction, and an engineered repair for sheared intake manifold ports that restored airflow and eliminated the misfires.

projects.problem: The car arrived with front-end collision damage and an engine that would not run cleanly. Before anything could be fixed, the real failure modes had to be separated from the noise.
projects.roleDetail: Everything: assessment, diagnosis, the repair strategy, fabrication, and assembly.
approach: Performed a comprehensive mechanical and structural assessment, identifying front-end collision damage and engine performance issues through component inspection and fault-code diagnostics.
Reconstructed the front-end assembly.
Engineered a repair for sheared intake manifold ports by precision tapping and installing vacuum valves and lines, sealed with high-temp epoxy.
results: Restored proper airflow through the intake manifold.
Eliminated engine misfires and returned the vehicle to running condition.
projects._photoGroupsNote: photoGroups makes labelled columns side by side. The 1st photo of every column shares a row, the 2nd photo shares the next row, and so on, so comparable photos line up and sit centred against each other. "width" sets how wide a column is relative to the others, so 1 and 1.7 means the second column is 1.7 times wider. "crop" shows a photo at a set shape ("1/1" square, "4/3", "16/9") trimmed evenly from the top and bottom instead of at its own proportions. "maxWidth" stops a photo filling its column, and is needed whenever a crop makes a photo tall. "59%" makes a photo in the After column exactly as wide as one in the Before column, because the After column is 1.7 times wider and 1 divided by 1.7 is 0.59. Use photoGroups OR photos, not both.

Owned design, pneumatic sizing, build, and validation of a 16-up leak test fixture for IP-rated RF surge protectors; sized four cylinders to apply 42.5 psi at FoS 1.3 over the customer spec, performed FEA to a ~680 lbf structural load, and increased throughput 300% to 16 units per 10-second cycle across 21,000+ units tested.
Supported end-to-end design and validation of EMI/RF protection components; applied CAD/3D modelling, GD&T, assembly, and bench testing with data acquisition to verify performance and reliability.

Own design and optimisation of the fuel delivery system; used CAD and FEA to improve combustion efficiency and structural integrity, and CNC machining to produce efficient components; achieved 414 mpg in competition.

Rebuilt the pressure side of a port-injection fuel system: replaced a 3.2 lb assembly that had cracked and leaked at multiple interfaces with a 2 L PET air charge bottle and a single machined aluminium adapter — roughly 97% lighter, cheaper, and faster to build.
Train Class B CDL-permit drivers in safe operation, defensive driving, and transit procedures, including instruction on bus mechanical systems.
Direct day-to-day operations of a 28-bus fleet, supervising drivers, coordinating dispatch, and resolving service disruptions to keep service safe, reliable, and on time.
